add.issue.name: The GUI ships React’s development build, unminified

edit.description.md:
`build-gui.mjs` runs esbuild with no `--minify` and no `NODE_ENV` define, so every shipped GUI — npm, SEA binary, and the one `npm run test:gui` exercises — serves React's *development* runtime and unminified source.

Measured on this branch:

- `dist/gui/main.js` 3.22 MB, of which `react-dom.development` is a part; the same bundle with `--minify --define:process.env.NODE_ENV='"production"'` is 1.20 MB (-63%), and `dist/gui` as a whole drops 15 MB -> 12 MB.
- A cold load of a 30k-event board over loopback: 3.08 MB of script, first ticket card at ~200 ms, network idle ~540 ms.

React's development runtime is not just bigger, it is slower: every render pays the dev-only checks and warning paths. That cost lands on the board, on the scrubber, and hardest on the diff panel.

The one thing lost is the pageErrors fixture's coverage of React's dev warnings (`source/test/e2e-gui/fixtures.ts` treats a `console.error` as a failure, which is how a style shorthand/longhand conflict gets caught). Keep an opt-in dev build for that.

add.issue.name: The GUI server sends no validators, so every reload refetches the whole bundle

edit.description.md:
`serveStatic` in `source/gui/api/api-server.ts` answers every request with `content-type` and the bytes — no `ETag`, no `Last-Modified`, no `Cache-Control`. So a reload refetches and re-parses 3.08 MB of script that has not changed, every time.

esbuild already content-hashes the split chunks (`chunk-*.js`, one per lazily-loaded Shiki grammar), so those are immutable by construction and can be served as such. `index.html` and `main.js` are not hashed and need a validator instead.

Worth more than it looks: the log panel is open while agents work, so the GUI is reloaded often, and the same handler is what a public-mode server (R2KHXNW) would answer over a real network.

add.issue.name: A commit’s diff opens every file at once, and the size guard is per file

edit.description.md:
Reported from use: large diffs take a long time to load.

The server is not the problem. Measured against a scratch clone of this repo's own history, over the real websocket:

| commit | files | server | payload | JSON.parse | painted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6722a2ea | 118 | 73 ms | 1.80 MB | 4 ms | **5406 ms** |
| 3bfe5f6b | 21 | 41 ms | 0.72 MB | 1 ms | 2629 ms |
| 4e08961b | 38 | 102 ms | 0.65 MB | 1 ms | 2571 ms |
| a954c15f | 6 | 31 ms | 0.22 MB | 0 ms | 1421 ms |

All of it is client-side rendering. `DiffPanel` maps every file of the commit to a `FileDiffView`, and the only brake is `isLargeDiff`, which asks whether *one file* exceeds 4,000 lines or 200,000 chars. A 118-file commit where no single file is large therefore opens all 118 and hands 1.7 million characters to the highlighter in one go — none of them collapsed.

Fix direction: budget across the commit, not per file. Open files until a whole-commit budget is spent, then collapse the rest behind the "show diff" notice that already exists, so the panel is usable immediately and the reader opens what they want.

Measured with the development React build; part of this cost goes away with the production build, so re-measure after that lands.

add.issue.name: The TUI re-derives a ticket’s seven virtual node ids with SHA-256 on every refresh

edit.description.md:
`virtualNodeId` (`source/lib/virtual-nodes/virtual-ids.ts`) is a pure function — `sha256(`${parentId}:virtual:${kind}`)` re-encoded as a ULID — and nothing memoizes it. `materializeTicketVirtualNodes` calls it seven times per ticket, and `refreshAffectedVirtualNodes` runs for every node a write touched and its parent, so the whole set is re-hashed on every replay and again on every interaction afterwards.

Measured at 3,000 tickets (21,000 ids): 345 ms cold, 17 ms memoized. That is why the TUI's replay costs ~3.5x the GUI's — at 200k events, replay is 0.94 s with virtual nodes on against 0.26 s with them off, and a read after a write is 0.08 s against 0.04 s.

The same function also recomputes seven *constant* ranks per ticket (`bigIntToHex(MAX_RANK / 4n)` and friends) — 11.9 ms per 3,000 tickets for seven strings that never change.

add.issue.name: Every event’s payload is cloned by zod’s looseObject just to read its envelope

edit.description.md:
`parsePersistedEnvelope` validates each log line against `PersistedEnvelopeSchema`, a `z.looseObject`. Loose means zod copies the whole object through — envelope *and* the payload it is not checking — so every event on every load is allocated twice.

Phase breakdown of one load of a 30,038-event board (100 ms total):

| phase | ms |
|---|---|
| readFileSync every log | 12.7 |
| split into lines | 2.3 |
| JSON.parse every line | 14.6 |
| **zod envelope parse** | **20.9** |
| getSortedEvents | 19.4 |
| payload decode + validation | ~30 |

The envelope is two fields — `v` a positive integer, `id` a `[string, string|null]` tuple. Checking them by hand costs a fraction of that and allocates nothing, and the quarantine reasons stay identical. This is on the cold-boot path of the TUI, the GUI server and the MCP server alike.

add.issue.comment.md:
Reopening with the measurement the last comment asked for, and taking the narrow version it named — memoize the per-file parse, keyed on (name, size, mtimeMs).

The two costs in the description have since been addressed: `getEdgeRef` holds an edge cache keyed on the log signature, and `boot()` skips the whole load-and-replay when `accountedSignature` still matches. What is left is every *other* reader of `loadAllPersistedEvents` — `loadMergedEventsBefore` (time travel), `loadEffectiveEventTimes` (:peek prev/next), `loadEventActors`, and the timeline index — each of which re-reads and re-parses every line.

Measured on a generated 30,038-event board (`source/test/stress`, never the real one):

- one `loadMergedEvents`: 100 ms, of which readFileSync 12.7 ms, JSON.parse 14.6 ms, zod envelope 20.9 ms, sort 19.4 ms
- the same call again, immediately: 88 ms, then 74 ms — nothing is remembered between them

At 200k events the load is 0.57–0.68 s, and scrubbing asks for a cut every 120 ms.

The cache is safe for the reason the comment gave: the log is append-only, so a size that has not moved is content that has not moved, and mtime catches a file a sync replaced wholesale. It needs nothing from outside `loadAllPersistedEvents`, so it cannot be defeated by `resetState()` the way a materialized-state cache would be.

Related tickets filed from the same measurement pass: C17HNZY (the zod envelope clone) and XXRMJ7C (the TUI's virtual-node id hashing).
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.name: The diff highlighter runs on the main thread; @pierre/diffs supports a worker pool

edit.description.md:
`@pierre/diffs` tokenizes on whichever thread it is given. `MultiFileDiff` takes a `disableWorkerPool` prop and the library ships `WorkerPoolContextProvider` plus a worker body at `@pierre/diffs/worker/worker.js` — but nothing in this client provides a pool, so every diff is syntax-highlighted on the main thread and the page is frozen for the duration.

Measured against a scratch clone of this repo's history, same build, same data — time from the files being in hand to the panel painted:

| commit | files | today | whole-commit budget only | budget + worker pool |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6722a2ea | 118 | 5595 ms | 2493 ms | **881 ms** |
| 3bfe5f6b | 21 | 2665 ms | 2633 ms | **661 ms** |
| 4e08961b | 38 | 2610 ms | 2690 ms | **642 ms** |
| a954c15f | 6 | 1401 ms | 1467 ms | **684 ms** |

The pool is the larger of the two by a distance, and unlike the budget it helps the ordinary commit as well as the pathological one — a six-file diff halves.

What it needs: the worker body built under a URL the browser can fetch (an esbuild entry point beside `main.js`, in the same run so the two share the lazily-loaded Shiki grammar chunks rather than shipping them twice), a pool sized off `hardwareConcurrency` rather than the library's default of 8, and the provider above the router so the pool outlives the routes that draw diffs.

Split from Z4MP3Y1, which covers the whole-commit budget — the same symptom, two independent causes.

add.issue.name: e2e-gui: a comment-count assertion over the whole log fails when another spec wrote comments first

edit.description.md:
`event-log.pw.ts` › "a comment line leads to the comment, not just its tab" counts `[data-log-tab="comments"]` rows across the **whole board's** event log and asserts exactly 2 — the two the test just wrote. Three specs write comments into the same per-worker repo (`comments.pw.ts`, `event-log.pw.ts`, `insert-image.pw.ts`), and a worker runs several files one after another, so the assertion only holds when this file happens to run first on its worker.

Reproduces deterministically, on `origin/main` as well as off it:

```
npx playwright test source/test/e2e-gui/comments.pw.ts source/test/e2e-gui/event-log.pw.ts --workers=1
  1) event-log.pw.ts:832 › a comment line leads to the comment, not just its tab
  Expected: 2   Received: 6
```

The file passes 14/14 alone. Across four full-suite runs of one unchanged branch it failed twice and passed twice, which is what sent me looking.

Fix direction: scope the count to the ticket the test created rather than to the log — the point of the test is that a comment line leads to *its* comment, and the "two of them, so landing on one is a different outcome from landing on the tab" reasoning in its own comment is satisfied by two comments on one ticket, not by two in the log.

Found while running the suite for the performance branch; nothing on that branch touches comments or the event log, and the same command fails on main.

add.issue.name: Decide: should the gate run one GUI pass against the development React bundle?

edit.description.md:
CC160K8 made the shipped GUI bundle React's production runtime, which is 3x smaller and faster at every render. React's dev-only warnings — a style shorthand fighting a longhand, a missing key, invalid DOM nesting, controlled/uncontrolled switches — exist only in the development runtime, and `e2e-gui/fixtures.ts` failing a test on any `console.error` was the only thing in this repo catching them. 62 of the 65 spec files assert `expect(pageErrors).toEqual([])`.

`npm run test:gui:warnings` builds the development bundle and runs the suite against it, so the coverage is reachable. What is not decided is whether anything runs it.

The options, and what each costs:

- **Nothing does.** The warnings are caught only when somebody thinks to run it. Cheapest; the repo has already been bitten once by a shorthand/longhand conflict (see the React-style-warning note in the GUI suite's history).
- **The pre-push gate runs both.** Doubles the browser suite, which is already the longest leg — about 1.5-2.5 min a pass on a quiet machine, more on a loaded one.
- **CI runs the dev pass, the gate runs production.** A red comes later but costs no local time. Needs a job.
- **A nightly or weekly run.** Cheapest that still catches things, latest signal.

Production React also minifies its error text, so the failures that do survive read as "Minified React error #418" — worth weighing.

Parked rather than decided alone: it is a trade between gate time and a class of bug, and that is the user's call.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `build-gui.mjs` now defines `process.env.NODE_ENV` and minifies, through esbuild's JS API rather than its CLI — a define's value is JSON, and the quotes around `"production"` would not have survived the Windows shell the CLI call used.

Measured on a 30k-event board over loopback: `main.js` 3.22 MB -> 1.20 MB (1.02 MB once the worker entry of MRVQD8E moved the highlighter core into a shared chunk), `dist/gui` 15 MB -> 13 MB, first ticket card 200 ms -> 138 ms, first contentful paint 104 ms -> 80 ms, script bytes 3.08 MB -> 1.14 MB.

What it costs: React's dev-only warnings — a style shorthand fighting a longhand, a missing key, invalid DOM nesting — exist only in the development runtime, and `e2e-gui/fixtures.ts` failing on any `console.error` was the only thing catching them. `EPIQ_GUI_DEV_BUILD=1` builds that bundle and `npm run test:gui:warnings` runs the suite against it. Whether the gate should include that leg is a decision, not a fix — filed separately.

Review also: `dist/gui` is emptied before each build. Every lazily-loaded chunk carries a content hash, so a rebuild left the previous set beside the new one and `build-sea.mjs` embedded both.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: the pool is provided by `WorkerPoolContextProvider` around the board's two routes, and `build-gui.mjs` builds `@pierre/diffs`'s own worker body as a second esbuild entry point beside `main.js` — in the same run, so the Shiki grammars both load on demand are one set of chunks rather than two. An entry point rather than a module importing it, because the package declares itself side-effect-free and a bare import of the body is tree-shaken away. Sized off `hardwareConcurrency` rather than the library's default of eight.

Time from the files being in hand to the panel painted, against a scratch clone of this repo's history:

| commit | files | before | + budget (Z4MP3Y1) | + pool |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6722a2ea | 118 | 5595 ms | 2493 ms | **881 ms** |
| 3bfe5f6b | 21 | 2665 ms | 2633 ms | **661 ms** |
| 4e08961b | 38 | 2610 ms | 2690 ms | **642 ms** |
| a954c15f | 6 | 1401 ms | 1467 ms | **684 ms** |

Two things review caught. The provider sat above the router, so the popped-out event log — which draws no diffs — started a window's worth of workers as it mounted. And the library does not report a broken pool: a worker that fails to load logs one line, leaves its `initialize` task unsettled forever and never drains its queue, so every diff stays blank where before there was a pool at all the same failure drew on the main thread. The factory now watches for that error and the diffs pass `disableWorkerPool`. `build-sea`'s asset check fetches `/diffs-worker.js` too — it walks what `index.html` references, and the worker is named by `main.js` at runtime.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `openableByDefault` / `pathsOpenByDefault` in `lib/utils/diff-size.ts` walk a commit's files in order and open them until a shared budget is spent, leaving the rest behind the "show diff" notice that already existed for the lockfile case. A file the per-file limit refuses does not also spend the budget, or one big file near the front would shut everything behind it.

Review caught that it was on the wrong surface. `DiffPanel` is the fallback for a commit whose subject carries no ticket ref — every commit in this repository carries one, so clicking the 118-file commit lands in the ticket's Code tab (`IssueCommits`), which had its own per-file filter and opened all 118 regardless. `SquashedDiff` did the same. All three now ask the one rule, with reviewed files filtered out before it rather than by it.

The budget charges both sides of a file. `isLargeDiff` takes the larger because it asks whether one file is outsized, where summing would call a modification large that an addition of the same file is not; this asks what a diff costs, and a diff reads both revisions. 500k, so a commit that would fit inside one large file is untouched.

Worth recording for whoever tunes this: with MRVQD8E's worker pool in place the budget is worth about 13% on the 118-file commit (780 ms against 894 ms) rather than the 2x it was worth alone. It stays because it is the only cap on how many file trees mount at once, and because the per-file component cost the pool cannot move is what is left.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `serveStatic` computes a sha1 ETag over the bytes it serves and answers 304 on a matching `if-none-match`. The tag is remembered against the file's size and mtime, which an append or a rebuild both move, so a matching request costs a `stat` rather than a megabyte. `no-cache` rather than an expiry: `main.js` and `index.html` keep their names across builds, so anything that let a browser skip the ask would serve a stale client after an upgrade. Under SEA there is nothing to stat and the assets are fixed for the binary's lifetime, so the tag stands for the process.

Verified against a live server: exact `If-None-Match` gives 304 with ETag and Cache-Control and no body, HEAD behaves, `/board/x` shares `index.html`'s tag, and touching the file forces a correct recompute.

Review found a crash in the same function, predating this: `GET /%` ended the process. `decodeURIComponent` throws on a stray percent, the request handler is an async function, and node answers an unhandled rejection by exiting — one curl from anything on the machine and the board server was gone. A path that will not decode is now a 404, and the handler is wrapped so nothing in it can end the process; there are three more `decodeURIComponent` calls behind it.

Not done, and deliberately: 383 of the 403 files carry a content hash and could be `immutable` rather than revalidated. That is a further win and a further way to serve a stale client, so it wants its own pass.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `virtualNodeId` memoizes in a module-level Map, and the seven field ranks are derived once instead of per ticket.

A full refresh of every ticket's virtual fields on a 3,000-ticket board: 71-77 ms before, 34-40 ms after. That is the pass the TUI makes on boot and again on every step of a scrub, since scrubbing re-materializes from scratch.

A cold boot moves less than the microbenchmark suggested — each (ticket, field) pair is hashed once either way — so the replay figure at 200k events is unchanged within noise. The win is every refresh after the first.

An unbiased review checked the memo for cases where the same (parentId, kind) must yield a different id — `:open` into another project, `resetState()`, time travel — and found none: ticket ids are ULIDs, so no cross-project key collision, and virtual ids are derived rather than persisted. It also measured the growth: ~10 MB transient and ~2 MB steady on a 3k-ticket board, TUI only, since the GUI and MCP both call `setVirtualNodesEnabled(false)` and never populate it.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `parsePersistedEnvelope` reads the two envelope fields by hand and returns the line itself. `PersistedEnvelopeSchema` stays as the one place the shape is written down, and `parsePersistedEnvelopeStrict` keeps it reachable; `event-envelope-parse.test.ts` holds the two to the same answer over every shape the load path can meet.

The envelope parse went from 20.9 ms to 2.1 ms per 30,038 events, and the load as a whole from 100 ms to 88 ms (69 ms measured through the boot path).

A differential fuzz over the two implementations, run as an unbiased review, found two shapes where they disagreed — both ordering bugs rather than performance ones:

- `v` past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. zod's `.int()` is a safe-integer check and `Number.isInteger` is not, so this build alone gave such a line a place in the causal forest. Two builds then derive different orders from one event set.
- A line with an own `__proto__` key, which `JSON.parse` produces. `looseObject` drops it, so every build shipped so far reads the line as its remaining keys and applies the event. Kept, it is a second key beside the action: `getPersistedAction` refuses the event and `sortEvents` stops recognising a genesis line as a root. An event older clients apply, this one would have dropped — straight into "never break a client that is already out there".

Both are in the CASES table and both fail without the fix. That line, and only that line, now pays for a copy.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `parsePersistedEventsFile` remembers what a log file parsed to, keyed on its size and mtime, taken before the read for the reason `logSignature` gives.

Two loads of a 30,038-event board back to back were 88 ms and 88 ms; they are now 88 ms and 31 ms. At 200k events the timeline's warm per-request cost went from 4.2 ms to 1.5 ms and its cold index build from 0.93 s to 0.69 s. Boot already skipped the load when the signature was unchanged; what this reaches is every other reader — time travel, `:peek prev/next`, the timeline index — and a scrub asks for a cut every 120 ms.

Review found the justification I wrote for using `mtimeNs` was false. Measured in this project's own Linux container: mtime granularity there is exactly 1 ms, so `mtimeNs` carries no more than `mtimeMs`, and 2668 of 2999 consecutive same-size rewrites were indistinguishable. It then reproduced an actual stale parse.

Fixed with git's own racily-clean rule: a file whose mtime is not yet a tick behind the read is not remembered at all. It costs nothing that matters — a file written this instant is the one about to be written again — and it is what makes the stamp a fact rather than a guess. There is a test that proves the cache serves hits at all, and one that proves the guard refuses, each verified red without its fix.

Also fixed: the bound counted events but not quarantine entries, so a log of nothing but corrupt lines sat there for free, and it bounded lines but not files. And a spread in `loadAllPersistedEvents` that predates this — an argument list has room for about 125,000 entries and then throws, out of a function whose contract is to return its failures.
add.issue.comment.author: QC69H5JC92YFHYHX16KNHQSNP9

add.issue.name: A binary file is drawn as a diff of its own bytes

edit.description.md:
A commit that added `docs/epiq-scrub.jpeg` draws the jpeg's bytes as 156 lines of diff — mojibake down the panel, one row per chunk of decoded binary, syntax-highlighted as if it were source.

Git already says it is binary and the code already reads the answer. `getChangedFileBlobs` parses `--numstat`, where a binary file is `-\t-\t<path>`:

```
$ git show --numstat --format= 2eb79e8df
-	-	docs/epiq-scrub-c.mp4
-	-	docs/epiq-scrub.jpeg
```

and maps both dashes to zero with the comment "A binary file's `-` counts as nothing changed line-wise, which is true" — true, and then the fact that it *was* a dash is dropped. The blob is read anyway, decoded as UTF-8, and handed to the highlighter.

So there are three costs, not one: it is unreadable, it is sent over the websocket in full (an image or a video, per file, per commit), and it is tokenized and laid out as text on arrival.

Fix direction: carry `isBinary` from the numstat line onto `CommitDiffFile`, skip reading the blob for those, and have the views say what the file is instead of drawing it. Git's own definition is the right one — it covers a `.gitattributes` `-diff` mark as well as a NUL in the first 8k, and it is the same answer `git show` gives a terminal ("Binary files differ").

Check all three front doors per the architecture skill: the GUI's commit panel, the ticket Code tab and the compacted view all draw `CommitDiffFile`; the TUI renders git's own patch and so may already be right.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `isBinary` is carried from git's own `--numstat` line onto `CommitDiffFile`, the blobs of such a file are not read at all, and the three views that draw one say what it is where the diff would be. Merged as PR #380 (two commits, rebase merge).

The dash was already being parsed and thrown away — `getChangedFileBlobs` mapped `-\t-` to a pair of zeroes with the note that a binary file changed no lines, which is true, and then nothing remembered that git had refused to diff it.

Measured on `c1c2e03c` in this history: 1041 KB of jpeg and png no longer read, no longer sent over the websocket, no longer decoded as UTF-8 and tokenized. The payload for that commit is 29.6 KB, all of it the one text file.

Git's own answer rather than a guess at the bytes, so it covers a `.gitattributes` `-diff` mark as well as a NUL in the first 8k — the same answer `git show` gives a terminal. That is deliberate and tested. It does mean a file marked `-diff` (a minified bundle, a generated file) is no longer commentable in the Code tab; its existing comments are listed under the notice rather than dropped, and they stay readable in the Comments tab.

The TUI needed nothing — it renders git's own patch, which already prints "Binary files ... differ" — and no `mcp/api` function returns a `CommitDiffFile`.

An unbiased review of the first commit found three things, fixed in the second:

- "Expand all" asked only whether a file was large, while the auto-open also asked whether there was a diff behind it. The two had agreed by accident while size was the only reason to refuse one, so a commit holding a jpeg offered "Expand all" with everything already open. `hasDiffToShow` says it once now and all three callers ask it.
- A binary row's header counted its comments and then drew none of them.
- A paragraph of an existing comment had been split around the new component.

It also checked the numstat signal against a real repo for a mode change, a symlink, an empty file, a tab in a path, a submodule bump and external diff/textconv drivers, and found one pre-existing failure it was careful to scope out: `getCommitDiff` errors on a submodule bump, because `--raw`'s gitlink hash is not a readable blob. Untouched here; worth its own ticket if anyone hits it.

Checks: 2034 unit tests, both typechecks, eslint, prettier, both container suites, browser 206/206, and CI green on the merged tree. The rendering was confirmed in a real browser as well.

add.issue.comment.md:

A comment's line is labelled `Commented: <the comment>` — the preview is capped at 90 characters and the test's comments are 19 — so filtering on that text picks out exactly this ticket's two, whatever else the worker's repo already holds.

It is also closer to what the test asserts. It clicks the *older* comment's line deliberately, to prove the mark lands on that comment rather than on whichever card the panel puts uppermost; it now names the older one instead of relying on the log's ordering to make `.first()` mean the right one.

Deterministic repro, before and after:

```
  before:  Expected: 2   Received: 5
  after:   15 passed
```

The other five log-line locators in that file were checked for the same shape and are fine: they use `toBeGreaterThan(0)` and `.first()`, so none asserts a global count. No production code changed.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: decided — a nightly run of the browser suite against the development bundle, not a second pass on the gate and not nothing. `.github/workflows/gui-warnings.yml`, merged as PR #384. Decided by me at the user's request rather than left parked.

Why nightly. The browser suite is already CI's critical path — three shards at about 3m30 — so a second full pass roughly doubles the most expensive leg on every branch push, forever, for a class of bug this repository has been bitten by once. A night's delay costs a morning; the runners cost every push anybody makes. Unsharded for the same reason: one runner once a night, with nothing waiting on the answer. `workflow_dispatch` too, so it can be run on demand before a risky GUI change.

The conventional shape for a React codebase is that dev-mode warnings come from component tests, which get the development build for free, while e2e runs against production for fidelity. This project has no React component tests, which is why the e2e fixture was carrying that job at all — so a scheduled extended run is the cheapest thing that keeps it.

It starts green: 206/206 against the development bundle on today's main, `react-dom.development` confirmed in the built bundle.

One bug found on the way. `test:gui:warnings`, added alongside CC160K8, built only the GUI — and the suite seeds each project by driving the real TUI, so on a fresh checkout it would have died at global setup for want of `dist/index.js`. The nightly job would have failed every night without reaching a test. It goes through `build:npm` now, verified from a cleared `dist`. Invisible locally, because a leftover `dist` made it look like it worked.

Checks: prettier + 2034 unit tests, typecheck, eslint, browser 206/206 against both bundles, and CI green on the merged tree.

add.issue.comment.md:
Reopened: the nightly trigger was the wrong shape and the user said so. "I don't think we need nightly runs for a solo project like this... I don't even work every day", then "only if there is a diff".

That is right and my reasoning was not. I took the convention for a team repository — a scheduled extended suite — and applied it to a project one person works on some days and not others. A clock bills for a runner on every day nobody touched the code, and reports a Friday regression on a Tuesday.

Changing the trigger to the change instead: `push` to `main` filtered to `source/gui/**`, `package-lock.json` (a React bump can introduce warnings with no source change of ours) and the workflow itself, plus `workflow_dispatch`. Zero runs on idle days, one run per merge that touched the GUI, and against a flat rebase-merged history a red run names one commit rather than a day's worth.

What it deliberately misses, written into the workflow: a warning introduced from `source/lib`, which the GUI draws from but which changes on most commits — watching it would fire nearly always and be worth nothing.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: the run is triggered by a GUI change reaching main, not by a clock. `.github/workflows/gui-warnings.yml`, merged as PR #385 on top of #384.

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - 'source/gui/**'
      - 'package-lock.json'
      - '.github/workflows/gui-warnings.yml'
  workflow_dispatch:
```

Zero runs on idle days, one run per merge that touched the GUI. Against a flat rebase-merged history that also attributes a red run to one commit rather than to a day's worth, which is better than the nightly would have managed.

`package-lock.json` is in the list because a React or renderer bump can introduce warnings with no source change of ours. `workflow_dispatch` stays for a deliberate run.

Deliberately not watched, and written into the workflow: `source/lib`, which the GUI draws from but which changes on most commits — a filter including it would fire nearly always and be worth nothing.

The decision this ticket originally asked for is in #384's comment above; this is the correction to its trigger after the user pointed out that a nightly schedule assumes somebody works every day.

add.issue.name: The per-commit view opens every commit in the reading layout, where the compacted diff already is

edit.description.md:
The Code tab switches between two views — the per-commit one and the compacted diff — and they are alternatives, not neighbours. The compacted view is where the whole change is read in one piece.

Which makes the per-commit view's remaining auto-expansion redundant: in the wide reading layout (fullscreen or docked to the bottom past LANE_VIEW_WIDTH) `expandAll={laneView}` opens every commit on arrival, and each one then fetches its diff and opens its files. A ticket with a dozen commits draws a dozen diffs nobody asked for, when the view beside it already shows the same content as one.

In the ordinary side panel a multi-commit ticket is already collapsed — `openCommitsOnArrival = expandAll || commits.length === 1` — so this is only the lane layout.

Fix: drop `expandAll`, so the per-commit view is a list to scan and the compacted view is the thing to read.

Leaving the lone-commit case alone: "with one there is nothing to choose between, so the tab opens it rather than waiting for the click that would", which has its own reasoning and its own test (`lone-commit.pw.ts`). Say so if that should go too — it is one condition.

add.issue.name: The primary button is bold as well as filled, which says the same thing twice

edit.description.md:
The primary button is set in 600 while the two beside it are 400, so a composer's row reads `cancel` · `file ticket` · **comment** — the last one shouting.

It already has a body where a default has an outline and a ghost has nothing, and that is the whole difference between them. The weight says the same thing a second time, and at 12px in this face it reads as emphasis rather than as hierarchy.

One weight for every button in a row. `fontWeight: isPrimary ? 600 : 400` in `Button.tsx` is the only place it is set, so this is the eight primary buttons in the client: the two composers, the two modals, the init screen's two, and the description editor's save.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: the per-commit view no longer opens every commit in the lane layout, and the switch carries the count. Merged as PR #386.

The history says why this was right rather than a matter of taste. `ES6E62N` (2026-08-30) opened every commit and file there "since it is for reading rather than scanning" — true while that was the only place a ticket's whole change could be read. `EEXWZN5` (2026-09-18) gave the Code tab a compacted view that shows it in one piece and took that job. The lane layout was then drawing a dozen diffs nobody asked for, one segment away from a view showing the same content as one, and fetching each commit's diff to do it.

In the ordinary side panel a multi-commit ticket was already collapsed, so this is the lane layout alone. The lone commit still opens itself — its own reasoning, its own test.

`Commits (4)` on the switch, reusing the count the Code tab already wears, so "undefined while in flight" is stated once and there is no wrong `(0)`.

No pair on `Diff`, and the reason is in the component: that count would be changed files, which only the compacted diff knows, and it is fetched when its view opens rather than with the ticket — deliberately, since building it reads every changed file's contents. Summing `--shortstat` per commit would double-count a file two commits touched. A number that arrives once the reader is already looking is not one that helped them decide to look. A count-only websocket message would fix that and is its own small piece of work if anybody wants it.

`fullscreen-lanes.pw.ts` asserted the behaviour `ES6E62N` added. It is inverted rather than deleted — it now pins that the lanes list the commits as the tabs do, that no diff is drawn until asked for, and that opening one by hand still opens its files — and it names both tickets so the change of mind reads from the test.

Checks: prettier + 2034 unit tests, both typechecks, eslint, browser 206/206.

add.issue.comment.md:
Reopened and closed again: the job's first real run failed, and the fault was the job's.

A GUI change reached main, the workflow fired as designed, and it reported five failures that pass everywhere else — an arrow left below the fold, a drag onto a commit dot, a paged-back window, a ticket narrowing, a comment line. Every one a test waiting on a state the app is trying to leave, which is what `playwright.config.ts` says suffers first when six browsers share four vCPUs.

`test:gui:warnings` never set `IS_CI`, so it took the local default of six workers and no retries where `test:gui:ci` takes two and one. It exports it now and installs the browsers the same way, so the workflow's separate install step went with it. Merged as PR #387.

That is the second defect in this one script; the first was building only the GUI, which would have failed the job at global setup on a fresh checkout. Both were invisible locally, where `dist` was already built and six workers have cores to run on — the lesson being that a CI-shaped script wants running the way CI runs it, not the way this machine does.

The job itself was sound throughout: it built, seeded and ran all 206 both times.
